previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman was admitted for evaluation of bright red blood per rectum and a sensation of a 'ball' protruding from the rectum during a grocery store visit. She had no pain but reported a history of constipation and fecal incontinence. Initial labs showed stable hemoglobin, mild leukocytosis, and low-normal platelets consistent with her known immune thrombocytopenia. The bleeding was attributed to hemorrhoids, possibly related to rectal prolapse, with no evidence of major gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Her chronic diastolic heart failure was stable, with no volume overload. The bowel regimen was intensified with docusate, senna, and polyethylene glycol to prevent recurrence. She was discharged home with services, advised to follow up with her PCP for colonoscopy scheduling and ongoing constipation management.

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ was admitted to the Colorectal surgical service one 
day prior to her repair of rectal prolapse.  She underwent a 
bowel prep using mag citrate and prophylactic antibiotics.  She 
tolerated the procedure well and the reader is referred to the 
operative note for further detail.  Post-operatively she was 
placed on the standard colorectal pathway.  She initially had 
some low urine output and received a few bolus of lactated 
ringers.  She responded to these well. In addition, her home 
diureties were started on POD1 and she had adequate urine output 
for the rest of her hospitalization.  Her diet was advanced to a 
clear liquid diet on POD1, however it was noted that she was 
extremely distended and she was backed down to sips.  She never 
had any emesis.  She was then advanced to a regular diet after 
passing flatus on POD3.  Given her history she was started on 
colace after having a small amout of bowel function. She was 
kept over the weekend due to slight distention and in the 
setting of not really having a bm again, so senna was started.  
A urinalysis was sent before discharge which revealed a UTI so 
she was started on Cipro. The rest of her home medications were 
continued.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital after an Alteimer procedure 
for surgical management of your rectal prolapse. You have 
recovered from this procedure well and you are now ready to 
return home. You have tolerated a regular diet, are passing gas 
and your pain is controlled with pain medications by mouth. You 
may return home to finish your recovery.
 
Please monitor your bowel function closely. You may or may not 
have had a bowel movement prior to your discharge which is 
acceptable, however it is important that you have a bowel 
movement in the next ___ days. After anesthesia it is not 
uncommon for patients to have some decrease in bowel function 
but you should not have prolonged constipation. Some loose stool 
and passing of small amounts of dark, old appearing blood are 
expected. However, if you notice that you are passing bright red 
blood with bowel movements or having loose stool without 
improvement please call the office or go to the emergency room 
if the symptoms are severe. If you are taking narcotic pain 
medications there is a risk that you will have some 
constipation. Please take an over the counter stool softener 
such as Colace, and if the symptoms do not improve call the 
office. If you have any of the following symptoms please call 
the office for advice or go to the emergency room if severe: 
increasing abdominal distension, increasing abdominal pain, 
nausea, vomiting, inability to tolerate food or liquids, 
prolonged loose stool, or extended constipation.
